extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, referees, and scholarly authors (scientists and research administrators)
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and evaluative standards for refereeing (peer review) of scholarly manuscripts and grant proposals, including referee selection, report content, editorial handling of disagreements, timeliness, and ethical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor initial screening: compatibility with scope and style
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor first checks a submission's compatibility with the scope and style of the journal before sending it for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a preliminary step editors take 'whether or not [a paper] is refereed' (Robert A. Day). It determines if the manuscript is appropriate and whether to choose it for refereeing; no further detail provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of referees (sources and methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are recruited from multiple sources: widely recognized experts, editorial board members, previous referees, authors suggested referees, and bibliographic/computer-assisted retrieval (e.g., Science Citation Index, Social Sciences Citation Index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may use personal acquaintances, lists supplied by authors, coded files of expertise, or literature searches/microcomputer search methods to find candidates; aim is to identify experts with relevant subject-matter competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of referees and balance for reliable coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Two referees are commonly chosen, but editors sometimes use additional reviewers; some argue more reviewers (even five to eight) can produce more reliable coverage of a manuscript's merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance referees so that one referee covers points the other misses; empirical judgments about the adequate number vary by journal/field and paper complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee report content and recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should provide specific comments and recommendations — typically accept, request modifications (revise), or reject — and often fill a form for comments and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should include specific comments for both the author and the editor, substantive critique, and a clear recommendation; editors commonly expect a prompt reply within a few weeks and concrete suggestions when recommending revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are expected to respond within a reasonable interval; excessive delays in refereeing harm authors (careers, priority, promotion) and frustrate scientific communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely reviews are valued; long lags are criticized and may be due to reviewers taking too long, overcritical behavior, or low prioritization. Editors should manage turnaround to reduce harmful delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core manuscript acceptability criteria: soundness, originality, significance, new perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael Gordon's set of criteria: 'First, it should be sound... It should also be original... it should be significant... it should contain some new perspective or observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees assess technical and methodological soundness, novelty (findings not previously published), importance/impact, and whether the paper offers a new viewpoint; manuscripts meet these to varying degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness and concreteness of criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should produce constructive, evidence-backed comments rather than invective or unsupported opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should identify flaws of logic or method with specifics, avoid ad hominem attacks, and where possible suggest remedies; editors often expect point-by-point responses from authors to referee comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling reviewer disagreement and editorial arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must manage disagreements among referees and between referees and authors by options such as relying on editorial judgment, sending the manuscript out again, asking referees to review one another's comments, or asking the author for a point-by-point response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedures: (a) consult additional reviewers, (b) send disputing referees' comments together, (c) ask authors to rebut/refute and resubmit, (d) editors may make final decisions after arbitration; no single standard — handled case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and prestige effects (including the 'Matthew effect')
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing can exhibit bias favoring well-known authors/institutions and disadvantaging unknown authors — a 'Matthew effect' where reputation affects acceptance likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be aware of affiliation/prestige bias; empirical evidence is limited but suggestive. Selection and anonymization policies may mitigate some biases; balanced referee selection helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and vested-interest bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers with vested interests (competing work, personal or professional stakes) may be overcritical or delay publication for benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should try to avoid reviewers with obvious conflicts; authors may suggest/oppose potential referees; policies should require disclosure and recusal when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical behaviors to detect and prevent (plagiarism, appropriation, misuse of privileged information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees and editors must guard against unethical acts such as plagiarism, appropriation of ideas/data, ghostwriting, and other abuses of the review process (examples include alleged appropriation of text or data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be sought before accusation; editors must investigate credible claims and take corrective action (corrections/retractions). Anonymity can complicate detection and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity versus accountability of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity of referees reduces accountability and can lead to uncivil or irresponsible reviews; some advocate for signed reviews or at least accountability mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance anonymity (which can enable frank critique) against potential for abusive anonymous invective; consider measures that increase transparency or require justification of critical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policies and formal rules (e.g., Ingelfinger Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may have formal editorial policies that determine publishability (e.g., prior publication restrictions like the Ingelfinger Rule) which affect editorial decisions independent of referees' scientific judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and referees should be aware of journal-specific policies about prior dissemination, duplicate publication, and news-media embargoes; editors enforce such policies in screening and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field- and journal-specific variation in refereeing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing procedures and norms vary across journals and scientific fields; what is appropriate in one area may be unsuitable in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should adapt peer review practices to disciplinary norms (e.g., number of reviewers, speed expectations, tolerance for speculative work); alternative outlets (specialized or speculative journals) exist for work outside mainstream norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for empirical evaluation of refereeing effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about refereeing effectiveness are often anecdotal; rigorous, controlled studies are scarce, so assessments of the system should rest on empirical evidence where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and journal managers should support empirical research on peer review (e.g., studies of agreement, bias, predictive validity) before broad policy prescriptions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee conscientiousness and complementary coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one solid, conscientious report is desirable and multiple referees may provide complementary coverage of a manuscript's strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should aim to select referees who together cover methodological, conceptual, and contextual aspects of the paper; lack of conscientiousness undermines the system's reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of the scientific record and communal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing is meant to ensure that publications meet communal standards — filtering inferior work, correcting errors, and preserving credibility of the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and referees should balance openness to novel ideas with responsibility to prevent publication of poorly documented or speculative claims lacking adequate support; the process may reshape manuscripts into better 'papers'.
